studies.market: NBA 99¢ bids behind observed final-score queues on November 18
studies.test: For all six recorded final-score queue trials from the first nine completed games, checked the winner YES and opponent NO books, then public sales through the earlier of the confirmed close or the study deadline. Each simulated bid arrived 33–35 seconds after the monitor first received matching final scores from NBA.com and ESPN.
studies.finding: The smaller observed queue ranged from 203,394.39 to 1,584,996.89 contracts. None of the twelve routes had enough subsequent sales to reach a five-contract bid behind the displayed quantity. On Memphis YES, the measured queue was 1,184,133.03 contracts and subsequent sellers traded 3,351.51 at 99¢. Earlier sellers traded 23,495.82 Philadelphia YES during the delay before the paper bid. The queue at the earlier time and the identities of cancelled bids are unknown.

studies.market: NBA halftime totals and spreads after the first half ended
studies.test: For the first nine final NBA games on November 18, checked four markets per game covering first-half and second-quarter totals and spreads. Verified the quarter scores against NBA.com and ESPN, then selected the nearest strike at least 4.5 points from the outcome, using ticker order to break ties. Counted executions from 30 seconds after ESPN's archived second-quarter end through the next five minutes. All 36 selected markets remained open for the full interval.
studies.finding: All 36 selected sides paid $1. There were zero buyer executions through 99¢. Sellers traded 6,048.68 contracts at exactly 99¢ across 20 markets. Two had enough selling for five contracts behind 1,000 shares and none behind 10,000. Median time from modeled arrival to settlement was 29.4 minutes. Earlier feed availability, queue position and account fills are unknown.

studies.market: Halftime bids on the November 16–17 NBA schedule
studies.test: Applied the same 4.5-point margin and five-minute public-trade window to an earlier schedule. Required the NBA quarter scores and ESPN period-end plays to agree before evaluating first-half and second-quarter totals and spreads.
studies.finding: Twelve games passed and one was excluded. All 48 selected sides paid $1. Buyers took zero contracts through 99¢, and sellers traded 22,614.82 at 99¢. Six markets had enough volume for five shares behind 1,000, and none behind 10,000. In the excluded Phoenix–Denver game, ESPN period-end plays implied Phoenix won the second quarter by eight. The official quarter score was 36–29, a seven-point margin. Kalshi settled Phoenix above 7.5 points NO. Two losing YES contracts traded at 1¢ each in the replay window.

studies.market: NHL game winners after the reported final score
studies.test: Compared NHL game reports, ESPN final plays and Kalshi settlements. Started 30 seconds after the later of the ESPN final play or the end of the minute printed on the NHL report. Counted non-block trades for up to five minutes after that reference or until market close. The historical timestamps describe the game and do not establish when a trader received the result.
studies.finding: In 20 completed games from November 15–18, seven markets were still open during the test. Only Dallas–Vegas had buyers take winning contracts through 99¢. One buyer took 5.92 Dallas YES at 98¢. The overtime goal and a video review share an ESPN timestamp. In a separate November 8–14 sample, 43 of 49 games passed score and timing checks. Of the 23 markets still open, zero had buyers take winning contracts through 99¢. Sellers traded 74,539.26 winner YES contracts at 99¢. Seventeen games had enough seller volume for five shares assuming an empty queue, seven behind 1,000 shares and three behind 10,000. For the seven, the median interval from modeled arrival to official settlement was 2.62 minutes. Actual queue position and fills are unknown.

studies.market: Discounted offers 15 minutes after Artnet-settled auction results
studies.test: Checked 224 thresholds across 29 artworks from November 16–17. Starting 15 minutes after the saved house result, required two consecutive one-minute exchange bars whose highest indicated-side offer was 95¢ or less. Checked up to 65 minutes after publication, picked the first qualifying decision per event, and broke simultaneous ties by lowest limit then ticker. Bars give prices without quantity.
studies.finding: Nine events qualified at 93–95¢ and all nine sides ultimately paid $1. Eight still showed the selected price or better throughout the following minute. The ninth had no next-minute quote. None had a public buyer execution at the limit or better from one second after the decision through the following minute. These prices justify watching confirmed depth beyond the initial announcement. Available shares and potential returns remain unverified.

studies.market: Late 99¢ Van Gogh offers after Sotheby's published $190.43M
studies.test: For five November 18 lots covering 45 thresholds, began 15 minutes after both house sources agreed and scanned until 10:14 p.m. Eastern. Checked 9,551 lot snapshots and public non-block buyer executions. Separately screened two independent books for up to five at 99¢, then checked for public purchases one to six seconds later. The sample covers result-side whole-contract book levels.
studies.finding: Through 98¢, no lot had a whole contract offered on the result side or a public buyer execution. At 99¢, buyers took 169.85 contracts across eight trades on Van Gogh above $180M YES and above $200M NO. Neither threshold's first repeated offer had a qualifying trade in the following five-second window. Among 170 repeated quote observations, one later window had a public purchase of one contract. The current pilot price ceiling is 95¢. No live or simulated profit was booked from this replay.

studies.market: Buying two sale-price thresholds on one artwork
studies.test: Paired YES on a lower threshold with NO on a higher threshold for the same lot under matching rules. One of those contracts pays $1 at any sale price under ordinary binary settlement. Compared the cost of buying both using whole-contract offers observed together. Repeated observations of the same book are counted separately.
studies.finding: Across five Sotheby's lots on November 18, 2,449 timestamped snapshots covered 180 distinct threshold pairs. Both legs had a recorded offer in 55,960 comparisons. Zero cost less than $1 before fees. The cheapest was $1.02 including the one-pair fee reserve. At 10:30 p.m. Eastern, three checks of all 123 pairs on nine Thursday lots found a lowest cost of $1.08 including the reserve, on Nicolas Party's Landscape. These samples leave gaps between observations.

studies.test: Read Kalshi's finalized markets and public trades. Compared exchange one-minute quotes from the start of November 17 Eastern through close on November 18. For the higher threshold, the cost to buy NO is $1 minus the YES bid.
studies.finding: Both settled NO. The $600K contract recorded zero lifetime volume. In 168 minutes with both required closing quotes, the cheapest pair cost $1.16 before fees. At 7:38 p.m. Eastern on November 17, lower YES cost 18¢ and higher NO cost 98¢. A high asking price for YES can coexist with an expensive NO when the spread is wide.

studies.market: Auction orders under the original $1 per-order and $5 total pilot limits
studies.test: Replayed the dated worker’s quantity calculation on saved order books. Checked for same-side public purchases at the limit or better one to six seconds after a second quote. November 16 and 17 archives recorded local receipt times. The historical checks cannot establish the exact order arrival or queue position.
studies.finding: On November 17, 2,729 archived checks covered 119 thresholds for 15 artworks at Phillips and Christie’s. Two offers were at or below 95¢. Both outcomes won, but neither offer had a second saved quote. After the Avery Singer YES quote at 95¢, a buyer paid 94¢ for one contract 1.752 seconds later. In the separate November 18 Monet example, the $1 cap allowed one of the 21 contracts at 64¢, with a 67¢ reservation including a fee allowance. Four later public trades bought 23 at 64¢. The dashboard rehearses the dated worker, compares its actual paper timestamps with public purchases and grades supported shares at official settlement.

studies.market: How much BTC distance was enough to justify a 98¢ bid?
studies.test: Measured both the chart reading and its five-second trend forecast against the strike with 45 seconds remaining across 5,316 settled markets. For November 4–17, checked public seller volume strictly below trial bids after a one-second arrival delay. Each comparison started with $1,000 and sized to 100 contracts per signal. The model charged standard taker fees as a cost sensitivity.
studies.finding: At a 98¢ bid, a fixed $55 buffer had three winning and one losing modeled purchase for a $92.55 loss. A 0.05% buffer had 14 winners and two losses for a $170.20 loss. At 0.10%, 0.125% and 0.15%, the same three purchases qualified and modeled a $5.59 gain in each case. At a 99.8¢ bid, the 0.15% buffer modeled $1.86 over both weeks. Historical book availability and the bot’s place in the queue were unknown. The forward paper rule continues to use 0.15%.

studies.market: Did the 64¢ Monet offer reappear after publication?
studies.test: For each of five November 18 Sotheby’s results, selected the cheapest offer through 95¢ on the published-result side in the first complete book within three seconds. Checked the exact price in the first independently timed follow-up book within 15 seconds, then counted same-price public purchases one to six seconds later.
studies.finding: Only Monet qualified. The book showed 21 YES at 64¢ at 1.574 seconds after the catalogue result and 23 at 11.011 seconds. Four purchases took 23 YES at 64¢ at 14.098 seconds. No eligible book measured the first one-to-three-second gap after the initial quote. The two book observations and later volume supported an illustration of 21 contracts, costing $13.78 with estimated fees and earning $7.22 if filled and settled YES. Both house reads used the same catalogue version. This retrospective example generated no bot fill. Forward sampling on the Artnet-settled lots records seven timed snapshots through 15 seconds, including empty books and missed observations.

studies.market: How long discounted bids lasted after a published auction sale price
studies.test: Checked 224 Artnet-settled thresholds on 29 sold artworks from November 16–17. Used separate $1,000 paper accounts, reserving up to $100 per artwork before checking for sellers. After a 2-, 10- or 60-minute delay, the first completed one-minute quote within five minutes had to remain above the bid throughout. Allowed one second for order arrival and counted only sellers strictly below the proposed price.
studies.finding: At 80¢, a two-minute delay and cancellation after one hour modeled 10 shares and $2 gross. Holding the bids through close modeled 36 shares, $28.80 spent and $7.20 gross on Rothko, Klimt and Monet. A ten-minute delay also modeled $7.20 through close. A one-hour delay produced zero matches on the eligible quotes. In a separate Sotheby’s sale on November 18, the monitor had two books per threshold showing an 80¢ bid could rest starting two minutes after publication. No sellers traded below 80¢ after those simulated arrivals through three hours after publication. Only the 95¢ Van Gogh bid had seller volume through it, modeling 11 shares and 55¢ potential gross pending settlement. Historical order priority and fills are unknown. Upcoming Artnet-settled Phillips and Christie’s lots have a separate prospective 80¢ paper account.

studies.market: Resting NO bids after a public auction withdrawal
studies.test: Used the later of publication and revision on the Warhol and Kahlo reports. Starting one hour later, required two consecutive completed minutes with a quoted NO ask above the limit throughout. Simulated a bid arriving one second later and counted subsequent sellers strictly below its price. Separate 80¢ and 95¢ scenarios each split $100 per artwork across all listed thresholds before looking for trades.
studies.finding: On the Warhol, 26.64 NO contracts sold below 80¢ on three thresholds after the corresponding bids could rest. That modeled 25 shares costing $20 and earning $5 gross through close, or $4.70 if charged estimated taker fees. A one-hour expiry modeled two shares and 40¢ gross. At 95¢ through close, 17 shares modeled 85¢ gross. The Kahlo had no qualifying sellers. Each scenario depends on one artwork at one sale, and the historical quotes omit depth. The forward paper accounts save the queue and subsequent sales for reported withdrawals.

studies.market: NBA full-game totals near an even chance with six minutes left
studies.test: Used the 2024–25 scoring distribution from 943 games to select one listed total per game. An entry required an estimated eight cents per share after taker fees. Checked the next 20 seconds for a public purchase of at least five shares at or below the modeled limit. The test included 698 quoted games in 2025–26 and 90 from November 1–17, 2026. Public trades establish prices paid by other buyers.
studies.finding: At five contracts per entry, the 2025–26 replay won 29 of 103 and lost $40.25. November won three of 14 and lost $7.98. Applying the actual public purchase prices still lost $27.29 and $6.59 after estimated fees. Updating the forecast with a more recent score also lost money in both periods. The market midpoint predicted outcomes more accurately in both samples. This directional rule has no demonstrated trading edge.

studies.market: NBA game totals with about six minutes remaining
studies.test: Used the first scoring play between 6:00 and 5:30 of the fourth quarter. The lower 1% scoring cutoff over the rest of 943 games in 2024–25 was 13 points. Allowing two points of room set the forecast at 11 additional points. In the following season, 922 of 924 scored at least 11. Selected one still-unreached, already-listed threshold per game that needed at most 11 more points. A $1,000 paper budget reserved up to 100 shares before checking sellers for 60 seconds.
studies.finding: All 423 eligible 2025–26 thresholds paid YES. At 98¢ with 30 seconds of latency, 16 games had enough seller volume below the bid to model 819 shares and $16.05 after estimated fees. Eleven of those had an archived ask range entirely above 98¢ during the arrival minute, accounting for 507 shares. A 90-second delay modeled $20.36. In November 1–17, 2026, all 69 eligible thresholds won, but no sellers traded below 98¢ under either delay. On November 18 the first two dual-source receipts arrived 43–46 seconds after the recorded plays. Neither one attracted a seller at 98¢ or less in the subsequent one-minute test. No realized profit.

studies.market: NBA full-game totals after the combined score clears the strike
studies.test: Examined November 13–17. In 34 of 36 games the final scores matched both sources. For 1,035 thresholds, matched scoring plays on NBA.com and ESPN by period, clock and both team scores. Used a four-point cushion and allowed 30 seconds after ESPN’s archived play time before checking five minutes of Kalshi trades. Historical timestamps do not establish live source availability.
studies.finding: All 519 crossed thresholds paid YES. Across 168 thresholds in 31 games, sellers traded 83,704.03 YES contracts into 99¢ bids. No YES buyer took an offer for 99¢ or less in the windows. With a hypothetical 1,000 contracts ahead, 22 thresholds in 14 games had enough selling for another five contracts. With 10,000 ahead, none did. The live paper study timestamps both scores, checks two books and tracks one 99¢ queue per game.

studies.market: Public withdrawal reports for Warhol and Kahlo at Christie’s
studies.test: Matched two November 17 reports naming the works to eleven Artnet-settled Kalshi thresholds. HENI published the Warhol withdrawal at 6:51 p.m. Eastern. For Kahlo, the conservative test used El Economista’s later 12:13 a.m. Eastern edit. Checked actual NO purchases from an hour later until the exchange close.
studies.finding: All eleven thresholds paid NO across two artworks at one sale. On Warhol, buyers purchased 24.50 NO at 95¢ or less, including a purchase at 87¢. On Kahlo, buyers purchased 3,815.16 NO at 98–99¢. Requiring two consecutive completed minutes with a qualifying quote before a subsequent whole-contract purchase left only Warhol Above $22M. The 95¢ scenario modeled one contract and 4¢ net after fees. The separate 99¢ scenario modeled 100 contracts and 93¢ net. Historical quotes omit size. The forward dashboard records quantities on two books for exact lot matches in HENI’s withdrawal list.

studies.market: BTC 15-minute contracts with ten seconds remaining
studies.test: Compared the latest chart reading and its five-second trend with the strike across 5,316 settled markets, September 23 through November 17 Eastern. Allowed two seconds of chart delay. For signals clearing 0.15%, checked seller trades strictly after a further second for a bid to arrive.
studies.finding: The side ahead reversed 78 times. The largest lead that reversed was 0.037%. All 1,478 signals clearing both checks settled on the predicted side. Sellers traded below 99.8¢ in ten of those markets, all of which had also qualified at 45 seconds. At 100 contracts per market and 99.8¢ per contract, that models $2 gross across eight weeks. One market traded exactly at 99¢ and none traded below it. Queue position, actual fills, fees and operating costs determine the achievable return.

studies.market: Exchange quote history for the $9.40 Kiefer paper gain
studies.test: Rechecked both NO positions against Kalshi’s finalized markets, all public trades on each threshold from one second after entry through close, and one-minute exchange quotes around each entry. For NO, the best offer is one dollar minus the best YES bid.
studies.finding: The 884-share paper purchase at 99¢ on Above $550K earned $8.23 on the ledger. Kalshi recorded a 1¢ best YES bid during that minute, corroborating a 99¢ NO offer at some point. The minute had zero trading volume and the market reported zero lifetime volume. The 125-share Above $850K position modeled $1.17 net. Its entry minute had no archived quote. Neither threshold had a public trade on either side after entry. The ledger confirms the payout direction and assumes execution of the quantities seen in the books. Future entries now get an independent depth check one to six seconds later.

studies.market: Funded auction bids after confirmed sales across four November 16–17 auctions
studies.test: Used saved house prices on 29 sold lots and all 224 mapped Artnet-based thresholds. Each 90¢ or 95¢ scenario started with $1,000. It reserved cash for simultaneous bids 31 seconds after each saved result, before observing seller activity. Bids expired after an hour or at close. Only whole shares supported by opposing public trades strictly below the bid counted. Unused funds returned at expiry and payouts returned at the recorded exchange settlement. The entry-minute quote range was inspected afterward to assess whether a bid could have rested.
studies.finding: At 95¢ and 20 shares per threshold, the one-hour scenario modeled 56 shares across five artworks for $2.80 gross. Holding bids to close tied up more cash and modeled only 31 shares for $1.55. For the one-hour case the archived ask range stayed strictly above the limit with a numerical offer for just one of the 56 shares. Twenty were on the Rothko Above $18M threshold, whose displayed NO offer was 87¢ during the arrival minute. A 95¢ order could have immediately matched there. The other 35 had incomplete arrival-price evidence. The 90¢ one-hour scenario modeled $5.60 gross on 56 shares, again with one share corroborated by a numerical offer above the bid throughout the arrival minute. The archive does not report size at that price.

studies.market: How long to leave a BTC bid open after the 45-second cushion clears
studies.test: September 23 through November 17, 2026 Eastern. Checked all 5,316 listed quarter-hour settlements. Every final chart candle matched Kalshi to the cent. At 45 seconds left, the latest chart reading and its five-second trend forecast both cleared the strike by 0.15% in 1,353 markets. Allowed one second for a bid to arrive and counted only subsequent seller-initiated trades strictly below the bid. Each price and duration used a separate $1,000 starting balance, with filled principal held until official settlement. The research script retains public trade IDs.
studies.finding: All 1,353 qualifying directions won. At a 99.8¢ limit, 16 windows showed 100 shares of seller volume below the limit within nine seconds, compared with 47 through close and 44 when canceling one second after the first failed cushion check. The corresponding gross results for 100 shares per order were $3.20, $9.40 and $8.80 over eight weeks. The 47 opportunities occurred on 31 days. A separate sensitivity sized each 99.8¢ through-close bid to the entire available cash balance before observing volume. With compounding, it produced $94.35 gross and exposed as much as $1,091.81 on a single outcome. Charging the standard taker fee formula on every modeled through-close purchase as a cost sensitivity leaves $8.46 before operating costs. At 98¢, two, five and four windows qualified, worth $4, $10 and $8 gross respectively. Historical books at bid arrival were unavailable. The forward comparison validates initial books and records cancellation delays and monitoring gaps.

studies.market: Testing a $55 BTC cushion against a reversal
studies.test: Among the same 5,316 closes, identified the losing forecast with the largest initial percentage cushion where the chart and forecast favored the same side. At 45 seconds before noon Eastern on November 14, the chart was $65,385.53 and the forecast was $65,376.41 against a $65,317.09 strike.
studies.finding: Both readings cleared the strike by more than $55. Kalshi settled at $65,316.74, so YES lost by $0.35. Between one and ten seconds after the signal, sellers traded 130,937.28 YES contracts below 98¢. The 0.15% rule skipped this market. An illustrative 100-share bid at 98¢ would have risked $98.

studies.market: BTC chart endpoint and executable prices
studies.test: Across 1,992 Kalshi closes on October 21–27 and November 4–17, the last Polymarket US one-second chart candle matched Kalshi’s expiration value to the cent in every window. A second average of the sixty chart readings differed in every window. On the separate October 28–November 3 week, tested a fixed five-second linear trend using only chart timestamps from before the simulated data request. Both the latest reading and projected endpoint had to clear the strike by 0.15%.
studies.finding: The last candle matched all 668 holdout settlements. Ten seconds before close, the trend picked 667 of 668 directions correctly. Of those, 171 signals cleared the cushion and all won. Across those 171 windows, public tape showed no 100-contract buy on the chosen side at 99.8¢ or less after the signal. At 45 seconds, 159 signals cleared the cushion and all won. One market had qualifying buys. None had a second qualifying purchase at least 1.2 seconds later. An exploratory seller-side check found three markets with at least 100 shares sold strictly below 99.8¢ between one and ten seconds after the signal. At 100 shares each, a 99.8¢ bid in all three would earn $0.60 gross if filled. Historical book state, actual fills, and live data arrival are unverified. The forward paper monitor timestamps chart receipts, checks both books before a simulated bid, and counts subsequent seller volume.

studies.market: 95¢ auction bids across all 45 Sotheby’s thresholds on November 18
studies.test: All 45 one-hour observation windows overlapped. An equal split of a $1,000 paper budget would have reserved 23 shares per threshold, or $983.25 across five lots. Counted only non-block sales strictly below the bid after allowing a second for arrival.
studies.finding: One threshold attracted sellers. Four trades sold 312.75 NO at 94¢ on Van Gogh Above $260M. The other 44 had zero sales at or below 95¢ on the indicated side. The equal split could model at most 23 purchases at 95¢ there, costing $21.85 and earning $1.15 if NO pays $1. The exchange had yet to settle the contract. This was the only threshold with zero visible shares queued at 95¢ or better on both reads. Future auctions test an empty-queue rule with an independent $1,000 paper balance capped at $100 per threshold. Neither model receives retroactive fills.

studies.market: Van Gogh 95¢ resting NO after the published $190.43M price
studies.test: The bot recorded Sotheby’s catalog and individual lot page agreeing on $190.43M. On Above $260M, two books had no immediately available NO offer at 95¢ or less and no visible NO bids at 95¢ or better. The prospective one-hour queue study recorded hypothetical arrival at 6:26:40.775 p.m. Eastern on November 18.
studies.finding: Three minutes and three seconds later, four non-block trades at the same timestamp sold 312.75 NO contracts to resting buyers at 94¢. A resting 95¢ bid would have offered a better price to sellers. The bot had no order in the queue, and the threshold remained unsettled at review. The same observation now covers published Phillips and Christie’s results on mapped Artnet-verified thresholds.

studies.market: Withdrawn Phillips lot after Artnet published its status
studies.test: Artnet's public Phillips catalog listed Derek Fordjour's Haberdashery, lot 17, as withdrawn. On November 18 at 7:29 p.m. Eastern, checked the unchanged Kalshi rules, all ten active strikes and three separate order books. The paper test used a 95¢ maximum NO price, the smallest whole-contract depth at the same price on all three reads, and a $1,000 budget across the ten strikes.
studies.finding: Only Above $250K qualified, with 58 NO at 95¢. Modeled cost was $55.30 with fees. A NO settlement would return $58 and earn $2.70, and YES would lose $55.30. All ten strikes were still open at entry. None of the five paintings with matched Sotheby’s prices had even one contract on the indicated side at 99¢ or less across all three reads. The paper entry tracks the withdrawn-lot hypothesis separately from bought-in lots.

studies.market: BTC cushion with 45 seconds to close
studies.test: Evaluated 1,992 settled quarter-hour contracts in October 21–27 and November 4–17, 2026 Eastern. At 45 seconds to close, held the latest proxy chart observation flat for the remaining part of the settlement average. Used only completed one-second candles from before a simulated request two seconds earlier. Required both spot and projection to clear the strike by 0.15%. Checked public purchases on the selected side from 44 to 35 seconds before close.
studies.finding: 690 signals qualified and all agreed with Kalshi settlement. Two markets had public buyer executions of at least 100 contracts at 99¢ or less. On November 15 the discounted purchases spanned 245 milliseconds. On November 17 they spanned 7.407 seconds and totaled 29,414.26 contracts. An exploratory fixed-limit calculation required two purchases of at least 100 contracts separated by at least 1.2 seconds and a fresh qualifying projection at the second purchase. At a 99¢ limit one market qualified, worth $1.02 at the more expensive print after modeled fees. At a 99.8¢ limit nine qualified for $3.01 total before operating costs. Those are overlapping scenarios. Historical prints cannot establish bot fills. The forward paper study checks two contemporaneous books and saves their depth.

studies.market: BTC quarter-hour contracts with a 0.15% cushion
studies.test: Evaluated all 1,328 finalized markets closing November 4–17, 2026 Eastern. Ten seconds before each close, used proxy chart candles completed before a simulated request two seconds earlier. Both the latest reading and the projected final-minute average had to clear the strike by 0.15% in the same direction. Checked the following nine seconds for non-block buyer executions of at least 100 contracts on that side.
studies.finding: The cushion passed in 536 markets, 202 in the first week and 334 in the second. All 536 agreed with settlement. The projected direction without the cushion was wrong 49 times. Of the 536 qualifying markets, none had a buyer execution of 100 or more at 99.8¢ or less in the remaining window. Two had such a purchase at 99.9¢, and neither had a second one at least 1.2 seconds later. Assuming 100 bought at each first print gives 18¢ of modeled profit after fees rounded up to a cent. There were no verified bot fills. The live dashboard also records the first chart observation with 6–10 seconds left whether or not an offer exists.

studies.market: NBA 99¢ bids after the final score
studies.test: Examined 122 games from November 1–17, 2026. Excluded 39 with incomplete or inconsistent timing or scores. For the remaining 83, NBA.com, ESPN and Kalshi agreed on the winner. Counted public trades on both team contracts from 30 seconds after the archived final play until five minutes after it or the market close, whichever came first.
studies.finding: 76 games still had an open market. In 75 of them, sellers traded winning contracts at 99¢ against resting buyers, totaling 1,332,515.22 contracts across 5,838 trades. No buyer crossed an offer in the window. On winner YES alone, 50 games had enough sales for five contracts behind 1,000 already waiting. Only 15 had enough behind 10,000. Historical data does not establish when the score became available or how many bids were ahead. The live paper study timestamps dual-source confirmation and records visible queues before measuring subsequent sales.

studies.market: NBA five-point leads with 35–50 seconds left
studies.test: Matched the exact ESPN play and its archived win probability to both Kalshi team contracts. Used five whole contracts per purchase, fees rounded up to a cent, and non-block taker executions five to fifteen seconds after the play, before the next recorded play. Excluded two play timestamps more than a day after the scheduled start. There were 29 usable windows. Historical play timestamps do not establish when a live reader received the score or probability.
studies.finding: Backing the leader returned 27 wins in 28 entries and a $0.71 modeled loss. Requiring a two-percentage-point margin between ESPN’s probability and the fee-inclusive purchase price selected no leaders. Applying the same rule to actual trailing-team purchases selected 25 entries, one win and a $0.73 loss on $5.73 of cost. The upset was Chicago at Golden State on March 10, 2026: with 47.5 seconds and a 115–110 lead, Golden State committed a shooting foul that gave Chicago three free throws. In the two regular-season archives, the leader won three of four games where the selected play was its shooting foul; in other play types leaders still lost three times. The live paper monitor now saves the play type, the team responsible and the exact-play probability when available.

studies.market: Van Gogh annual auction record after the November 18 sale
studies.test: Compared the $117.18M 2026 record threshold to the $190.43M Sotheby’s catalog and lot-page receipts. Checked every non-block annual-market purchase from the later receipt through 6:47 p.m. Eastern. The separate $1,000 paper strategy requires both source pages to show the same qualifying sale on new reads, unchanged annual market terms, and matching available YES size across two recent books.
studies.finding: Three annual YES contracts traded at 98¢ from 5.24 to 12.18 minutes after the later source receipt. At 19 minutes 55.678 seconds, nine transactions at one timestamp bought 7,290.04 YES at 99¢. A separate snapshot had shown that same size for sale. At 99¢ a $1,000 account could fund 1,009 contracts for $999.61 including an estimated 70¢ fee. A YES payout would net $9.39 before operating costs. The paper strategy recorded no entry in this window. Subsequent Sotheby’s responses had closed lots without a visible price, and the original 99¢ block disappeared. Kalshi’s annual and lot markets were still open at the check.

studies.market: Resting bids after the first published Sotheby’s price
studies.test: Exploratory replay of all five November 18 artworks. Selected each threshold with no whole offer through 95¢ in the first complete post-publication book within three seconds. Modeled a five-contract bid at 95¢ arriving one second after the snapshot. Counted public sales strictly below that price through five minutes after publication. Each hypothetical purchase is charged the full 95¢ plus a conservative taker fee. The replay uses subsequent trades by others.
studies.finding: Van Gogh was the only artwork with qualifying sales. After the published $190.43M price, 24.08 YES above $180M sold below the limit, and 403.62 NO above $260M sold below it. The five-contract cap limits the illustration to ten contracts, $9.54 total cost and 46¢ net if both outcomes settle as indicated. Monet had buys from available offers. Renoir, Cézanne and Pissarro had neither result-side buyer executions through 95¢ nor sales below the resting limit after modeled arrival. The new Phillips and Christie’s recorder preserves the first book even when the indicated side has no offer; those contracts use Artnet for settlement.

studies.test: The bot recorded five YES above $120M at 81¢ ($4.11 including fees) when bids for higher Polymarket ranges summed to 87.3¢. Rechecked all 108 subsequent archived pre-auction Kalshi snapshots for the cost of selling those five contracts and reconciled the first later public buyer with the paper entry.
studies.finding: The price difference still qualified in 83 snapshots. No snapshot offered a profitable exit on all five shares. The best exit modeled a 48¢ loss. Shortly before the auction the YES ask was 98¢ while the best bid was only 18¢. A public buyer paid 81¢ for ten shares about 39 minutes after the paper entry. Both Sotheby’s pages subsequently reported $111.01M, pointing to a $4.11 paper loss if Kalshi settles accordingly.

studies.market: Post-publication liquidity on three additional artworks
studies.test: Sampled all nine Kalshi thresholds at fixed times for Renoir, Cézanne and Pissarro. Required an exchange timestamp after the first public sale price and at least one whole contract. These observations were scheduled before any of the three results.
studies.finding: Sotheby’s catalog and corresponding lot pages agreed on Renoir at $27.5M, Cézanne at $111.01M and Pissarro at $24.2M. Six usable snapshots per lot in the first 31 seconds showed no offers through 99¢ on any of the result-indicated sides. The original, slower book collector missed its three-second window on all three lots. The additional snapshots provide the evidence for the empty books.

studies.market: How long the November 18 auction offers lasted
studies.test: For Monet and van Gogh, checked non-block buyer executions on the indicated side of all 18 thresholds in the five minutes after our first public sale-price receipt. For Renoir, Cézanne and Pissarro, an additional observer samples all nine thresholds at receipt and after 1, 2.25, 4, 7, 15 and 30 seconds. It excludes snapshots whose exchange timestamp could predate the result. These samples are separate from the original three-second test.
studies.finding: For Monet above $20M, a second snapshot 11.011 seconds after publication showed 23 YES at 64¢. Another 23 traded at 64¢ at +14.098 seconds. The first and second Sotheby’s reads had the same cached generation. There were no buyer executions at 95¢ or less on the sale-price-indicated sides from +15 seconds through five minutes. For van Gogh, one NO above $260M traded at 94¢ at +27.484 seconds. For Renoir, Sotheby’s catalog and lot page agreed on $27.5M. All six independently timestamped snapshots between +1 and +30.2 seconds had zero whole contracts offered through 99¢ on the indicated sides.

studies.market: Monet and van Gogh after the November 18 sale price appeared
studies.test: Compared the first public Sotheby’s result with the first complete Kalshi order book timestamped after its receipt and captured within three seconds. At the cheapest outcome supported by the result through 95¢, counted public buyers at exactly that price from 0.25 to 2 seconds after receipt of the quote. This timing rule was chosen after reviewing Monet. Renoir, Cézanne and Pissarro were designated for forward validation at 6:27 p.m. Eastern, before their first monitored results.
studies.finding: Sotheby’s catalog first showed $20.23M for Monet. At +1.574 seconds, 21 YES contracts above $20M were offered at 64¢. At +2.110 seconds, 22 YES contracts traded at 64¢. The bot recorded no fill on that offer. Buying 21 at the displayed price would cost $13.78 including an estimated 34¢ fee and net $7.22 if Kalshi settles YES. For van Gogh, Sotheby’s published $190.43M. The first eligible book contained zero offers through 95¢ on the indicated sides.

studies.market: Bitcoin distance from the threshold at 98–99¢
studies.test: Screened 3,396 finalized Kalshi quarter-hour markets from October 14 through 5:45 p.m. Eastern November 18. Replayed all 21,170 public non-block purchases of at least one contract at 98–99¢ in the final ten seconds. Used completed one-second candles from the Polymarket US chart available by timestamp 1.4 seconds before each trade. Assumed the last reading persisted for the unfinished portion of the settlement minute. Historical candles are a proxy, and their live arrival times are unknown.
studies.finding: 102 markets contained a qualifying purchase. None cleared a 0.15% cushion on both the latest reading and projected average, including all 504 purchases of at least 1,000 contracts. The largest cushion across all purchases was 0.03032%. Without the cushion, the first large purchase won in 80 of 81 markets. Starting with $1,000 and modeling 1,000 contracts per entry, the October 16 loss left too little cash for later purchases. Eight entries were affordable and the ending balance was $118.22 after modeled fees and before operating costs. The guarded replay had zero entries and zero trading profit. The live paper study continues with the original cushion.

studies.market: Losing Bitcoin purchases in the final ten seconds
studies.test: Rechecked every 98–99¢ buyer execution in the last ten seconds of two markets previously known to contain a losing purchase. Used the first single execution of at least 1,000 contracts on either side to determine the historical rule’s entry.
studies.finding: On October 16 at 5:15 a.m. Eastern, the first qualifying purchase was 1,001 YES at 98.2¢ with 5.98 seconds left. The final average was $82,163.26 against $82,163.44 required. A 1,000-contract entry cost $983.24 including modeled fees and paid zero. On October 31 at 10:15 a.m. Eastern, the first qualifying purchase was 3,027 NO at 98¢ and won. In that same market 5,775.13 YES contracts traded at 98–99¢ and lost, including 2,039.22 contracts at a single timestamp, although the largest individual losing print was only 647.03. A backtest requiring a single large print can select a different side from one that combines depth across price levels.

studies.market: A second large Bitcoin purchase before close
studies.test: Rechecked every one of the 35 markets with a 1,000-contract buyer at 98–99¢ in the last ten seconds, November 4 through 5:45 p.m. Eastern November 18. Looked for a second non-block buyer of at least 1,000 on the same side at the same or a cheaper price, at least 1.2 seconds later and still before close.
studies.finding: Four of 35 markets had a second qualifying print. The observed gaps were 2.28–4.02 seconds. Buying only at those four second prints modeled $57.71 net after fees and before operating costs. The remaining 31 had no comparable second purchase in the window. Public trades cannot establish how long unfilled offers persisted. The separate live paper test requires 1,000 contracts at matching prices across two fresh order books and enough available paper cash to purchase them.

studies.market: Bitcoin final-ten-second purchases in an earlier week
studies.test: Applied the same 98–99¢ price band, size requirements and fee calculation to all 664 finalized quarter-hour markets closing November 4–10 Eastern. Used the first qualifying public buyer execution per market, including fractional-cent prices.
studies.finding: At 1,000 contracts, 21 purchases qualified and all won, producing $280.14 of modeled net in this week. At 100 contracts, 27 purchases qualified and all won, producing $37.34. Across both date ranges, 35 of 1,400 markets had a qualifying 1,000-contract execution. The median first purchase was 7.955 seconds before close. Replaying the public purchases chronologically, paying modeled taker fees and releasing funds at exchange settlement, grew $1,000 to $1,463.48 before operating costs. Each purchase cost $981.38–$990.70. The current forward study records repeat visible offers at one contract and their displayed depth.

studies.market: Bitcoin at 98–99¢ in the final ten seconds
studies.test: Across 736 finalized 15-minute markets closing November 11 through 5:45 p.m. Eastern November 18, took the first non-block buyer execution in the final ten seconds at the required size, including fractional-cent prices. Modeled standard taker fees rounded up to a cent per purchase.
studies.finding: At 100 contracts, 16 markets qualified and all won, giving $23.39 modeled net. At 1,000 contracts, 14 markets qualified and all won. Eight of these markets had a qualifying 1,000-contract purchase at exactly 98¢ or 99¢. Using $1,000 starting cash and crediting payouts at exchange settlement, the larger model spent $984.17–$990.70 per entry and ended at $1,183.34 before operating costs. A single lost entry would exceed all 14 gains combined. A separate forward paper strategy now records one contract and visible depth when two fresh order books agree on an offer in that final window.

studies.market: Bitcoin final-minute favorites observed in paper trading
studies.test: Reconciled the first two 98–99¢ entries recorded by the live paper monitor with Kalshi settlement and the complete non-block public trade record for each final minute. Counted same-side buyer executions of at least one contract.
studies.finding: On November 18, the 5:00 p.m. Eastern NO entry at 98.7¢ earned 1.21¢ after modeled fees. The 5:45 p.m. YES entry at 98.4¢, recorded with 46.63 seconds left, lost 98.52¢. Kalshi’s final average was $62,431.08 against $62,433.25 required. After that paper entry, buyers traded 4,330.22 YES contracts at exactly 98.4¢, including 25 contracts 0.52 seconds later. Neither market had a qualifying purchase of the recorded side at 98–99¢ in the final ten seconds. Two paper entries produced a combined loss of $0.9731. Public trading volume establishes that other buyers traded at the observed price.

studies.test: On 29 sold artworks, started a 15-minute watch at the first whole-share buyer execution through 95¢ at least 30 seconds after the saved sale result. Required another 30 seconds before counting a later purchase. Counted at most one later purchase per artwork.
studies.finding: Nineteen artworks had an initial purchase. Eight had a qualifying later purchase somewhere on the same artwork. Four had one on the initial threshold and seven had one on a different threshold, with three artworks in both groups. On Rothko, one Above $13M YES traded at 94¢ and 5 minutes 43 seconds later 42 Above $17M YES traded at 93¢. Taking the first later trade per artwork with a five-share cap modeled 32 shares costing $29.93 and paying $32, before operating costs. Actual traders’ executions establish prices and sizes, but another order may not have filled.

studies.market: Auction prices confirmed by a second market
studies.test: Used Polymarket’s recorded winning-range close plus 30 seconds on five November artworks. Checked later Kalshi buyer executions only where the entire range implied one side of the threshold.
studies.finding: 36 of 43 Kalshi thresholds had a determinate side. Two artworks had subsequent whole-share buys through 95¢. Buying up to five contracts at the first qualifying trade per artwork modeled ten contracts costing $9.53 and paying $10. A third artwork had a buy through 99¢. The live monitor records its own first receipt of a final Polymarket range before measuring later Kalshi offers.

studies.test: Compared four works in Christie’s October 14 London results with the same works in Artnet’s October top ten. Checked the premium-inclusive sale-currency amount and each publisher’s US-dollar equivalent.
studies.finding: All four GBP prices matched exactly. The US-dollar equivalents differed by $86,446 to $280,969. For Kandinsky’s Das bunte Leben both sources reported £31,560,000. Christie’s converted that to $41,785,440 and Artnet to $41,504,471. These are publisher comparisons. Rothko was sold directly in USD and its Kalshi settlement matched the Sotheby’s result.

studies.test: Across 224 settled thresholds on 29 sold artworks, counted opposing non-block taker executions of at least one share from 30 seconds after a recorded result until close.
studies.finding: Resting participants bought the winning side below 95¢ in 42 executions across ten thresholds on seven artworks, totaling 1,071.44 contracts. Four artworks still had such purchases after one hour. None of the qualifying executions was exactly 95¢. The prospective monitor checks whether a 95¢ bid could have rested, records the visible queue and measures subsequent seller volume for one hour. Public executions alone do not establish where a new bid would have filled.

studies.test: Checked all 224 settled thresholds on 29 sold artworks across four November 16–17 sales. Timed whole-share, non-block buyer executions through 95¢ from the first recorded auction-house price.
studies.finding: After an hour, 12 artworks across all four sales still had a qualifying purchase. After six hours, three artworks did. Warhol’s Flowers sold for $18,217,500. A buyer took three Above $17M YES at 61¢ about four hours and 49 minutes after the recorded result. Taking the first eligible purchase per artwork after one hour, capped at five shares, modeled 34 shares, $31.12 in cost and $2.88 net after fees. This assumes getting the actual buyers’ prices and sizes. Operating costs are excluded.

studies.market: Published auction prices and Artnet-based settlement
studies.test: Compared auction-house results saved on November 16–17 to Kalshi’s final numeric settlement values on contracts naming Artnet. Counted each artwork once across four sales.
studies.finding: All 29 distinct sold lots matched to the dollar, including 14 at Sotheby’s, seven at Phillips and eight at Christie’s. All 224 thresholds settled in the indicated direction. The Rothko matched at $17,705,000. This measures price agreement on the observed sold lots. Trade availability and the timing of Artnet’s own update were outside this comparison.

studies.test: Matched settled Kiefer paper entries to Kalshi trades and checked all ten thresholds from the first recorded paper NO until market close.
studies.finding: The two late paper entries modeled 1,009 shares and $9.40 net on one artwork. The 884-share NO on Above $550K accounted for $8.23. That threshold reported zero lifetime trading volume. Across all ten thresholds, the only non-block NO taker executions of at least one whole share after the first paper signal were two one-share fills at 83¢ on Above $500K at 9:38 a.m. ET on November 18. Both settled NO. The visible quotes and these small executions provide different evidence about attainable size.

studies.test: Twelve selected follow-up order books from the November 16 auctions, matched with the earlier book and the next 30 seconds of Kalshi trades.
studies.finding: Light Leaks sold for $5 million. On Above $3.5M YES, two snapshots 0.229 seconds apart each displayed 130 whole contracts at 91¢. A buyer took eight at 91¢ 25.316 seconds after the second snapshot. Those eight would have earned about $0.67 after estimated fees. This was the sole matching trade across these follow-ups. The snapshots lack exchange generation timestamps and establish neither continuous availability nor a bot fill. For Rothko Above $18M NO, two snapshots 37.952 seconds apart each displayed 51 at 87¢, with no matching buyer execution at an overlapping price in the next 30 seconds.

studies.test: November 11–17, 2026. Used the first uncorrected same-day afternoon NWS report from eight cities to pick its corresponding Kalshi range. Checked whole-share YES purchases starting one minute after release and ending within an hour or at the next report.
studies.finding: The recovered sample contained 51 station-days. The forecast won 49 of 50 finalized markets. Only three markets had a public YES purchase of five or more at 95¢ or less. At five contracts each, San Francisco at 92¢ modeled a 37¢ gain and Seattle at 77¢ a $3.92 loss after estimated fees. New York at 94¢ remained unsettled. Seattle’s preliminary 59°F became an official 61°F. This sample shows a loss of $3.55 on the two finalized purchases even with the high overall forecast accuracy. The forward paper test requires independently refreshed order books.

studies.test: Matched the lot-page symbols retrieved on November 18 to 14 archived November 16 sold prices. Checked the five contract-linked November 18 lots before the sale.
studies.finding: Eleven of the 14 earlier lots display an irrevocable-bid symbol. For six of those eleven the standard premium calculation exceeded the published price. All three unmarked lots matched. Sotheby’s says a fee for a successful irrevocable bidder can reduce the reported price. Bidder identity and individual fee amounts were unavailable. All five upcoming lots displayed the symbol before the sale. The dashboard records the disclosure available at each forecast and the size of the deduction that would erase the forecast’s margin.

studies.market: Sotheby’s live bids and buyer’s premium
studies.test: Applied Sotheby’s published New York fine-art premium tiers to archived November 16 bids. Compared projections with published sale totals, Kalshi settlements and public trades.
studies.finding: The standard formula matched 8 of 14 published totals and overstated 6 by $100,000–$1.3 million. On the final displayed bids alone it predicted 23 additional YES thresholds, of which 2 settled NO. The Rothko estimate was $18.505 million and its published result was $17.705 million. In the archive of live bidding, two successive readings produced 17 premium-only threshold signals across eight artworks. All 17 settled YES. Six had a public YES buy through 95¢ during the sampled windows, worth $0.48 total if one share had filled at each first eligible trade after estimated fees. Historical trades cannot confirm our place in the book.

studies.test: Earlier replication on October 21–27, 2026, using the same size, price, and final-ten-second rules.
studies.finding: Of 664 finalized markets, 68 had a qualifying taker purchase at size 100 and all won, for $6.12 modeled net. At size 1,000, all 64 qualifying purchases won, for $59.52. Across the three sampled weeks there were 148 qualifying markets at size 100 and $13.32 of modeled profit. One losing entry would have erased that amount. Resting participants matched size 100 on the 99.9¢ side in 653 markets in this earlier week. Public executions reveal neither our hypothetical queue position nor whether the offers were available on two reads.

studies.test: All 1,328 finalized quarter-hour markets closing November 4–17, 2026, Eastern time. Used the first non-block trade of the required size in the final ten seconds at exactly 99.9¢, once per market and role.
studies.finding: Buyers took at least 100 contracts in 80 markets. All 80 purchases won, worth $7.20 total at 100 each after estimated fees. The two weeks contributed 47 and 33 wins. At 1,000 each, 79 qualifying buys won for $73.47 modeled net. A single loss at 100 contracts would cost $99.91. In 1,324 markets a resting participant on the 99.9¢ side matched at least 100 contracts, and in 1,250 markets at least 1,000. All those sides won. A new bidder would have joined a queue with unknown priority. The dashboard now measures subsequent volume against the visible queue and tracks a separate paper test for immediate purchases.

studies.test: Checked the 35 latest finalized hourly events on each index at 4:13 p.m. ET on November 18, 2026. Compared lower YES and higher NO under matching rules.
studies.finding: All 70 events had consistent payouts across their thresholds. These events span six trading dates. Historical results validate the payoff relationship only. The first live scan found zero pairs offered below $1 across 3,220 open contracts. New paper entries require two fresh order-book checks and a positive margin after reserving whole-cent fees on each leg.

studies.market: Van Gogh annual record and individual lot
studies.test: Cost if one leg of the first 16 paper pairs filled alone
studies.finding: The pair cost $15.85 including entry fees. If only the 16 annual YES shares had filled, the repeated bids in the entry books would have returned $14.29 after modeled sale fees, an 87¢ loss. If only the painting NO shares had filled, there were no bids to exit and 69¢ of entry cost was exposed. The modeled gain if one leg per pair ultimately pays is 15¢. These were paper entries.

studies.test: Five settled November lots with mutually exclusive Polymarket price ranges
studies.finding: The winning range fixed the direction of 36 of 43 Kalshi thresholds. All 36 agreed with official settlement. The other seven fell within the winning range or on its lower boundary. Two hours before each sale, historical chart prices across ranges summed to 105.1%–148%. The public trade history yielded zero direct taker sales of five or more YES shares in the windows around those comparisons. These records establish outcome agreement but cannot reproduce the live strategy’s bid depth or five-share fills.

studies.test: Sale schedule versus last trading time on November 18
studies.finding: Kalshi listed 15 Artnet-verified thresholds for the sum of prices at Sotheby’s 12-lot evening sale. Their posted closing times were 4:28–4:29 p.m. Eastern, ahead of the auction’s 6 p.m. start. A strategy based on the published collection total had no scheduled trading window. The five individual artwork markets had later closing times.

studies.test: Public buyer executions in 14 windows the paper monitor sampled
studies.finding: In the final minute, 538 favorite-side buys of at least one contract printed at exactly 98¢ or 99¢ across four markets. All four first buys won, worth 7.44¢ combined at one share per market after modeled fees. The live monitor recorded zero qualifying entries. In the final ten seconds none of the 14 markets had a qualifying buy. One had 13 buys above 99¢. Trade prints cannot establish that the same prices were available to the bot.

studies.test: November 18 pregame match-winner prices
studies.finding: Two books implied a 58.38–63.04% chance for BORRACHEIROS after removing their margins. Two Kalshi reads showed 60¢, requiring 61.68% to break even at the modeled fee. Axorfy Gaming needed 73.42% at 72¢ against a 69.46–73.95% range. Neither cleared both books. Bookmaker update times were unavailable. No paper entry.

studies.test: Official settlement of November 16 bookmaker screen
studies.finding: Of ten distinct matches, six were ahead of their scheduled start when the screen was archived. After fee rounding, Apogee was the sole positive pregame estimate and settled NO, a modeled loss of 45.73¢ on one YES. The two larger positive estimates, JUMBO TEAM and Team Spirit, were already past scheduled start. Results use one quote per event and provide no evidence of a repeatable pregame edge.

studies.test: Both ways to back a five-point leader, accounting for score delay
studies.finding: In the 2025–26 regular season, the first qualifying buy on either leader YES or opponent NO five to fifteen seconds after the play matched 22 games. Twenty-one won for a modeled $0.1973 loss at one contract per game. Waiting at least ten seconds gave 16 wins in 17 and a $0.4405 loss. The next season through November 15 contributed five winning entries worth $0.0651 combined. The archived postseason games contributed one win worth $0.0186. Public prints do not establish when our monitor could have entered.

studies.test: Delayed start on two-book auction replay, November 16
studies.finding: Untitled (Shipwreck) was the only lot with qualifying depth on two archived order books. Starting 30 seconds, one minute or three minutes after the first recorded sold price still showed one contract at 91¢ and one at 92¢ on two subsequent reads. Each delay modeled $0.159 net after fees. Starting five minutes late found zero qualifying pairs in the available archive. These delays reuse the same two shares.

studies.test: 3 p.m. station readings before the afternoon climate product, November 11–17
studies.finding: Across 28 station-days, 34 thresholds crossed on 20 station-days and all agreed with settlement. From 3:01 p.m. local standard time to the earlier of the afternoon product or 4 p.m., no whole-contract same-side taker buy at 99¢ or less appeared. An earlier check started one minute after the first supported crossing and ran up to one hour, ending by 3 p.m. All 33 earlier thresholds agreed with settlement and none had a qualifying buy. Both checks used the same four stations and dates.

studies.test: First 1¢ or 2¢ taker buy in the final minute, November 4–17
studies.finding: Across 1,328 resolved markets, 469 had a qualifying non-block buy of at least one contract. Seven won. At one contract per entry the modeled net after fees was −$1.5172. November 4–10 lost $2.3870 and November 11–17 gained $0.8698. The 1¢ and 2¢ entry groups both lost money across the full period.

studies.test: Price chart confirmation before final-ten-second buys, October 7–November 10
studies.finding: Across 3,324 windows, 68 first 98¢ or 99¢ closing trades were favorite-side taker buys of at least one contract. They won 66 times and lost $0.9491 after modeled fees. The projection from 46 one-second Polymarket US chart prices called 40 of 68 outcomes correctly. Requiring a 0.05% margin in the buyer’s direction selected two trades. Both won, for $0.0279. Historical chart retrieval cannot establish when those prices became available.

studies.test: First 98¢ or 99¢ print in the final minute, November 11–17
studies.finding: At one contract per market, the 98¢ cohort won 171 of 176 and lost $1.73 after modeled fees. The 99¢ cohort won 51 of 52 and lost $0.52. Each cohort uses the first qualifying print on either side. The separate 1–2¢ experiment checks whether a buyer could obtain the low-priced side.

studies.test: Artnet unsold settlement precedent
studies.finding: For the Williams FW16B at Sotheby’s on November 16, Kalshi recorded Unsold and finalized all six thresholds NO. The six thresholds share one auction result. This is one precedent for a bought-in lot. Withdrawals are tracked separately.

studies.test: Station confirmation before the afternoon report
studies.finding: Across the same 28 station-days, time-stamped aviation observations supported 41 of 49 threshold signals using a one-degree cushion. All 41 agreed with final settlement. None had a qualifying public buyer through 99¢ in the screened hour. Central Park’s 52°F six-hour maximum crossed midnight. Same-day station evidence reached only 48°F, leaving the below-50°F NO unconfirmed.

studies.test: Four stations, November 11–17 afternoon climate reports
studies.finding: A one-degree buffer identified 49 crossed thresholds across 28 station-days. All 48 finalized markets agreed. Only the Central Park high below 50°F had qualifying buyer executions one to sixty minutes after issuance. The first timestamp included 250 NO contracts at 98–99¢. The afternoon report gave 52°F, but the next National Weather Service report and The Weather Company both recorded 47°F. As of November 18 the market was closed with settlement pending.

studies.test: Price limits, competing buyers and repeated order books
studies.finding: Across 105 settled thresholds, allocating $1,000 to observed buyer executions after 30 seconds modeled +$104.36 at a 95¢ limit and +$88.07 at 99¢. At 95¢, $80.16 of the modeled gain came from Rothko. The archive sampled books for 78 thresholds. Two successive books 1–30 seconds apart supported just two shares on one artwork, for +$0.159 after modeled fees. Reserving the cheapest share for another buyer left +$0.0748. Archive coverage was incomplete.

studies.test: Five-point leads with 35–50 seconds left in regulation
studies.finding: 2025–26 replay of Kalshi buyer executions. Of 1,220 quality-screened games, 226 had missing or reversed late-game timestamps. The remaining games produced 43 signals. In 21 games a buyer paid up to 99¢ five to fifteen seconds later, before the next recorded play. Twenty leaders won. One share per matched game modeled a 22¢ loss after standard fees. Golden State led Chicago 115–110 with 47.5 seconds left, traded at 92¢ and lost. Live paper testing requires two displayed offers and a fresh score.

studies.test: November 16 · live bid strictly above an Artnet threshold
studies.finding: Across 58 archived live-bid observations on ten artworks, seven artworks crossed 14 thresholds. All 14 settled YES. All six public executions in the sampled windows were YES buys at 97¢ or 98¢ across three thresholds. No whole-share buy qualified at 95¢ or less. The archive did not capture the live asks for those crossings. The November 18 forward test compares bids with fresh offers on five lots that settle directly from Sotheby’s.

studies.test: November 16 · repeat purchases after a public result
studies.finding: Across 24 thresholds with buys at 95¢ or less at least 30 seconds after a result, 11 had another eligible buy at least a minute later. Grouping simultaneous fills, a five-share cap gave $6.29 modeled net for first buys and $17.47 including repeats. Using the full printed quantity up to $1,000 of cash gave $103.13 modeled net on $999.87, with $708.83 of cost on the Rothko alone. This assumes taking the place of actual buyers. Available depth at those times is unknown.

studies.test: November 16 · 14 artworks across two sales
studies.finding: All 105 thresholds settled on the side implied by the published sale prices. Buyers took that side at 95¢ or less on 25 thresholds after the result was seen. On three thresholds a buyer traded at the exact price seen in an archived book 1–30 seconds earlier. Capping entries at five shares per threshold and the smaller of observed and traded size gave seven shares, $6.46 modeled cost and $0.54 modeled net. Archive coverage was incomplete.

studies.test: November 17 · timing of public buys after recorded desktop signals
studies.finding: By November 18 at 1:32 p.m. Eastern, 20 thresholds on eight artworks had a buyer on the indicated side at 95¢ or less at least 30 seconds after a signal. The first eligible buy arrived at least an hour later on seven thresholds. Desktop delivery times and displayed size at those later trades are unknown.

studies.test: Earlier week, same 98¢ or 99¢ closing-buy rule, Nov 4–10 ET
studies.finding: 85 of 86 qualifying buys won across 2,016 windows. Modeled net was $0.24 after fees at one share each. On Nov 8, a 47.48-share Down buy at 98¢ had a block timestamp nine seconds before noon ET. Up won. Across both weeks, 164 of 165 buys won and modeled net was $1.38. None of the first qualifying buys reached 1,000 shares.

studies.test: Both legs winning when opening prices differ by at least 0.20%
studies.finding: The exchanges confirmed both legs paid in 48/104 and 109/209 wide-gap windows in the two weeks used to choose the rule. In a separate earlier week, 43/92 paid both legs. Historical entry prices are unknown. The forward paper test allows up to $13 total for ten pairs after fees, and requires two fresh quotes within 30 seconds of opening. At that price, normal matching settlement pays $10 or $20.

studies.test: First 98¢ or 99¢ taker buy in the last ten seconds, Nov 11–17 ET
studies.finding: 79 qualifying buys across 2,016 resolved windows. All 79 won, for $1.15 modeled net after fees at one share each. Nov 17 contributed 8 wins and $0.13. The preceding six days contributed 71 wins and $1.02. None of the first qualifying buys reached 1,000 shares. Block timestamps can lag matching, and a past buyer’s price does not establish available depth.

studies.test: Shared quarter-hour settlements, Nov 4–17 ET
studies.finding: All 1,318 comparable closes reported identical final Bitcoin prices and different opening strikes. Ten additional Kalshi closes had no corresponding US listing. The live test prices ten lower-strike Up and higher-strike Down pairs after fees. Both legs must fill and the exchanges must use the same closing value for the $10 minimum payout to hold.

studies.test: Reconstruct official opening and closing values, Nov 17 ET
studies.finding: Across 288 markets, the chart reconstruction never matched both official values for the same market. The live strategies use published contract strikes and order books.

studies.test: Public result versus settlement source
studies.finding: 105 thresholds on 14 earlier lots matched. Several thresholds shared the same auction result.

studies.test: Official publication before trading closes
studies.finding: 337 checks found no Nov 17 count before the last poll, 26 seconds before close.

studies.test: Next-season replication
studies.finding: 14 winning selections. The sample is too small to establish a 97.6% win rate.

studies.test: Held-out final-minute game states
studies.finding: The historical screen narrowly passed. Executable depth and timing remain unverified.

studies.test: Opening bookmaker odds versus Kalshi
studies.finding: The March replication failed. Earlier simulated gains did not hold up.

studies.test: Prospective forecast and order book
studies.finding: The registered forward test ended without a qualifying entry.

studies.test: Coinbase-based probability model
studies.finding: Historical prices used a proxy for the CF Benchmarks index. Historical depth was unavailable.

studies.test: Buy complementary outcomes
studies.finding: Basket entries were counterfactual. Filling every leg at the indicated price was unverified.

studies.test: Magnitude forecast versus quoted price
studies.finding: One forward paper position. Sequence-specific probability calibration remains uncertain.
